title: Larb Gai
subtitle: thai minced chicken salad
excerpt: Larb gai is a Thai minced chicken salad dressed with fish sauce, lime juice, chilli, and toasted rice powder. It is light, sharp, and full of fresh herb flavour. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Larb originates in northern Thailand and Laos, where it is eaten as an everyday salad. Gai means chicken. The toasted rice powder is a key textural element that thickens the dressing slightly.

glossaryTerms.definition: A minced meat salad from northern Thailand and Laos. It is dressed with lime juice, fish sauce, chilli, and toasted rice powder.
A pungent fermented condiment made from fish and salt. It is the primary seasoning in larb and many other Southeast Asian dishes.

Toasted rice powder is made by dry-frying uncooked rice until golden, then grinding it. You can use chilli flakes as a shortcut if you skip this step.

items.prepNote: toasted in a dry pan, used in place of toasted rice powder

content.text: Toast the chilli flakes in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan over medium-high heat, cook the minced chicken, breaking it up as you go, until cooked through and lightly browned. About 6 minutes.
Transfer the warm chicken to a bowl. Add the shallots, chilli, and spring onion.
Add the fish sauce, lime juice, and sugar. Toss to combine.
Sprinkle over the toasted chilli flakes. Taste and adjust the dressing.
Serve at room temperature with steamed rice or lettuce leaves for wrapping.

attrs.solution: Add a pinch more sugar and a few more drops of fish sauce. The balance in larb shifts quickly so adjust in small amounts.
Mince it yourself from thigh rather than buying pre-minced breast. Thigh has more fat and stays moist after cooking.
Dress the salad while the chicken is warm. Cold chicken does not absorb the lime and fish sauce as well.

content.text: Larb is the national dish of Laos and a staple in northern and northeastern Thailand. It is eaten as an everyday meal in homes and at market stalls. The pork version is common in Laos; the chicken version is more popular in Thailand. It is nearly always served with sticky rice.
